utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, a preliminary matter to be raised on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, everyone. Could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next, Your Honour, if we can go into private session. The part we were on was in private session last.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM279, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. We'll now first move into private session, and Mr. Ivetic will then continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If we can call up in e-court your 92 ter transcript, P1614 under seal, but not broadcast the same to the public. And if we could turn to page 11 of the same. And if we could focus on line 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to read for you a part of your answer from the 92 ter transcript and ask you some questions following it, so please follow along. "A. In order to explain that, I have to go back to 1992. The unit, as such, was established -- founded from a number of enthusiasts, mainly radio amateurs and officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, or, rather, former JNA officers who at that time were serving as officers in the BH Army. They started with modest equipment, and the unit grew to its full size in mid-1995, numbering, on average, 50 to 60. There was no professional-quality equipment either imported or inherited from the JNA. We just adapted and souped-up devices we had in our radio clubs, adding amplifiers, preamplifiers, and other components, and we managed to enable these devices eventually to monitor one channel from one site." Now, you've already explained to us that the modifications were done by the civilians, the ham radio operators. The question I want to ask you is a technical one: Is it correct that civilian-grade equipment, radio equipment, works on different frequencies than does military-grade equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct in stating that civilian grade radio equipment cannot -- cannot access military frequencies with the existing parts that are within a civilian radio unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want a brief answer, with the existing components, no, they can't, because every service gets their own frequency, and when you acquire equipment, be it for the air force, for ham radio operators, or professional military, it is done, but it is mechanically possible to add certain assemblies to broaden the range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I want to continue with the rest of your answer here in this 92 ter transcript to ask you about from line 12 onward: "Our capacities were modest, but they were used to the full. We had in our unit former JNA officers specialised in communications, and the core of the unit was made up by ham radio operators with 10 to 40 years' experience." And I want to ask you, sir, with respect to the former JNA officers specialised in communications, how many such officers did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, after all it was 18 years ago, but before I joined that unit and before I took up my position, I know for sure they had five or six high-quality officers from the former JNA. I know about two of them for sure who specialised in electronic reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you recall, could you tell us how many ham radio operators with 10 to 40 years' prior experience did you have in that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot hold me down to a particular number, but everybody who worked there were for the most part ham radio operators or people who had done that job in the former JNA, in Yugoslavia. We had one young man who worked at the installation in the south for the former JNA. We had one man who is now perhaps 75, and many others who had won awards and had enormous experience. We had one engineer, Tomo Trojak, who was the brain of the whole operation. We had another engineer of electrical engineering, Miralem. I cannot tell you how many, but there was a great number of the radio -- members of the radio club Banovici, from Tuzla, Gradacac, and other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there also individuals in the unit who did not have neither any prior experience in communications within the JNA nor any experience as amateur ham radio operators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as far as the staff were former ham radio operators, we've had some evidence at this trial of the role that the Bosnian Muslim ham radio operators had in relation to reporting the dire situation in 1994 in Gorazde which turned out to be overstated. That is, I believe, at transcript page 7928 to 7932. Did any of these former ham radio operators working for this unit that you have described come previously from working within Gorazde enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was no way, no opportunity. I'm almost sure nobody came from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about a different aspect of this, and to do so I'd like to have 1D1079 in e-court, and for the start, if we could look at page 1 together. While we wait for that, sir, you'll see the -- or I'll present to you the document is dated 1995 and it's from the foreign military studies officer of the US armed forces and is authored by Lieutenant-Colonel John E. Sray, and it relates to the Bosnian civil war, and he talks of ham radio operators in Bosnia. And if we can move to page 7 of this document, we can examine together one thing that he says. If we look at footnote number 4 and I'll read for you, sir, so you get the translation of what is said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, where is the footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Footnote 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Endnote 4, I apologise. It's endnote 4. It's in the middle of the screen right now. "Rumours persist that the Bosnian Muslim government has hired some of these public relations firms to conduct media campaigns on their behalf in the US and Europe. Former President Carter was berated when he noted that the American public only knew one side of the story in Bosnia but his statement stands as a concise and astute summary of the content analysis available in the press. One of the best examples of Bosniak propaganda occurred during the battle for Gorazde in April 1994. The Bosnian Muslim government convinced the world that the BSA demolished the town and inflicted numerous civilian casualties. (See, for example --" And then he lists US media, British media, German media, and French media, and then continues: "The international media dutifully interviewed and subsequently printed accounts of refugees which government officials made available to them. Unfortunately, most of the media failed to corroborate these stories. The press also broadcast reports from a Bosnian Muslim ham radio operator whom they insisted had to be authentic due to the accuracy of his reports pertaining to the NATO bombing during the fighting. Verification of these events later proved this reporting to be highly inaccurate, but the media had already moved on to further stories. Most of the damage that was done in the enclave had actually occurred almost two years prior to the battle when Muslims had conducted their own ethnic cleansing and burned out the Serbs' houses. As for the ham radio operator, no one who is hold up in a basement, as he claimed to be, can accurately describe events taking place on the battle-field. Rather, this person simply monitored the unsecured radio transmissions of UNPROFOR personnel who were controlling the NATO air-strikes. He then mixed these elements of truth with his own propaganda to deceive the media. In fact, no conclusive evidence exists that the ham radio operator was even based in Gorazde." And now I want to ask you, sir, I need to know if the ham radio operators that worked in the unit were ever involved with this type of activity, that is monitoring unsecured radio traffic and adding their own elements of propaganda to the same to achieve deception of the media, whether about Gorazde or about any other event or location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours that was a very long question, and if that could be broken-down in parts, and first of all, it also mentions ham -- the report itself -- the document itself mention a ham radio operator, and I think it is only fair to the witness if the identity at least, if the witness has knowledge of -- of such person before he could make any comments on what appears to be an Internet article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, it's a document of the United States Army. It's not an Internet article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Second of all, I'm asking about his -- the persons that were in the unit, whether they had engaged in similar activities. The identity of the ham radio operator which was never, I believe, known is irrelevant to the question. I'm asking about this type of activity, this type of behaviour that is being reported, whether the operator -- when the ham radio enthusiasts that were part of the unit ever engaged in such activities, and I think it's relevant and germane to this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- Mr. Ivetic, if you take step-by-step. The first question put to the witness whether anyone came from Gorazde. Now, even without reading this long report, whatever the source is, whether it's Internet or whether it's United States military, you could have asked the witness whether he is aware of any operator at any time adding anything to what he technically had listened to, and then on the base if the witness says, "Yes, I have knowledge about that," then of course he could tell us. If he says, "I've got no knowledge about it," then you could have some follow-up questions, one or two, such as are you aware that a similar thing was at least reported to have happened in Gorazde, and then we do not need to read pages and pages of reports. This is the way I suggest you would proceed. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, my question objectionable or not? I'd like to get an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited you to -- I -- I suggested to you that you would proceed in the way I indicated, and that would need a rephrase -- rephrasing the question, and if you have done so, we'll know whether there's any objection to the new question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I have a ruling on the objection of my standing question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what Mr. Ivetic read to you, that is about operators adding information to what they listened to. Did you have any similar experience ever in the team in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I appreciate Mr. Ivetic's efforts. However, first of all, I have to say that I believe this text has nothing to do with me or the work I was engaged in. We never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd please answer my question and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never added anything. We did not work that way. We were not engaged in propaganda. We were on the receiving end. We could not even transmit. Nobody ever added anything by way of any propaganda or anything else. I speak from experience, because it was monitored at a lower level and in two facilities, so the two were never aware what the other one was monitoring at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you have any further questions in this field, feel free to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My original question: Do you know if any ham radio operators that you had in your unit previously had engaged in these activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can go back to your Rule 92 ter transcript, P1614 under seal, and not broadcast the same. And we'll be looking at the bottom of page 9 of the same, leading on to perhaps page 10. And if we could focus on line 20 on this page. And it reads as follows, sir: "A. It all depended on the amount of equipment that was available at a given point in time. Since our unit was providing support to intelligence structures and, to that end, gathered information, it was never manned 100 per cent. On average, in the northern facility the tasks were performed by a platoon of approximately 15 men. They worked according to the following system: They would spend seven days in the facility and then seven days at home. It could change depending on the frequency of traffic, or [sic] they could spend 10 or more days in the facility, and this mostly happened in the summer of 1995, and then the subsequent 10 days at home. The workload was enormous. One worked 'round the clock under very difficult conditions, with poor equipment and poor training -- or, rather, poor clothing, I meant. And this was especially the case in the winter. There was no heating. Old heating stoves were used, if only just to keep the equipment in working order. "A similar situation prevailed in the southern facility as well. This facility was even more difficult to access, especially in the winter. It was also manned by a platoon which monitored radio-relay communications with approximately 12 to 18 men; on average, 15. They had the same work regime." Now, first I'd like to ask you, you say that the stations were not manned 100 per cent, but you have not stated what percentage the situation depicted. Could you tell us as far as the manning of the stations was concerned what portion of 100 per cent was actually staffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be precise in mathematical terms, but there was the unit establishment which changed from time to time. For the most part it was between 80 and 120 people per formation on paper. If one takes that at the moment we had between 80 and 90 people as per establishment, and if indeed on the spot there were only between 50 and 60, then you can do the maths for yourself to reach the percentage of the staffing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And little further down on this page, I believe it's not the part that's not visible on the monitor. If we go down a few more lines, you talk about that each shift was 24 hours in length, and I want to ask you: How many hours during a 24-hour shift did a particular operator work sitting at the receiver/scanner listening to communications without a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At each facility they had a roster in principle. It was pinned on the wall just simply to be there, but in my view, each operator worked on average between 15 and 18 hours manning the device. We knew more or less that right after midnight there would be little traffic, so some men would go in to sleep for five or six metres. It was all within the radius of 5 metres. If there is an increase in traffic, the people were awakened. You need to understand that it was wartime. It was not like in peacetime; otherwise, I could tell you how many people one would need and what sort of equipment you would need, but that was what it was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same question now for the operators that would be sitting down and listening to prerecorded transmissions on the UHER tape device. How many hours during a 24-hour shift would a particular operator be sitting working on that machine listening to communications and writing them down without a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to repeat there were no others. They were all the same people. They all sat down together, listened together, eat and drink together. They only had to make a few steps to take the notebooks to the encryption unit which was next door. That's where everything took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that operators could and did work on two machines at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is a bit, well, not necessarily unclear, but difficult to answer. Before that I have to tell you that a person had two devices in front of him. One was RRU 1 and the other RRU 800. Each work station had two, and they did not change work station unless they needed to help their colleague in his own work. Every person had two machines in front of them. They were the UHER devices. Everyone knew who was to man each work station and who was then supposed to replace them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mean to say that your unit had a RRU 800 device and a RRU 1 device? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have in mind professional military equipment, we did not, but these were modified amateur devices. One could monitor channels, that is to say, communication between 610 and 950; whereas, the other one could follow the frequencies between 230 and 270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. The devices, they depict the frequency range covered by that device. Is that -- or is it a specific piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are modified ham radio devices, Mr. President. A Kenwood 450, an ICR 100. It's all in the notebooks which work station used which device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the reference to RRU 800 and RRU 1 mainly refers to what frequency is covered by that -- covered by that modified equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many channels or frequencies could each the northern and the southern stations follow at any one time simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can say -- well, four workstations by 2 channels times 8. So 16 channels at both facilities. So at the moment when they are recording, at any given time they could only record up to 16 channels. As for scanning, they could cover well over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the playback of prerecorded tapes of transmissions, could you tell how many tapes be listened to simultaneously for purposes of writing them down into a notebook at any given time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listening to the tapes, depending on the number of people who were at the facility. So between four and eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can briefly turn to page 13 of the Rule 92 ter statement and focus on lines 15 through 21, I'd have a question to ask you about this. And you're quoted here as answering as follows: "After we identified -- or, rather, discovered participants in the traffic, we would proceed to record the communication. People could not memorise and then note down what they heard, so they first had to make a recording, then play it back and listen, and note it down. Such information was written down into station log-books according to the recipe of the former JNA or in our working notebooks, because we did not have any dedicated documents for writing this down." Now, this answer leaves me a bit confused, because on the one hand it seems to imply that the procedures of the JNA were followed but also at the same time they were not followed. Could you please clarify for us whether the unit followed the prescribed procedures set forth by the JNA for memorialising these communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't want to be critical of anyone, but there may be small mistakes occurring in the process of interpretation. In principle, we used the documents of the former JNA to create this mosaic, the jigsaw puzzle, because it was easiest way to do so. Since we did not have proper documentations with rubrics and columns, we used notebooks for that purpose. Perhaps I'm not expressing myself all too well, but we followed the procedures used by the JNA, but, however, it was translated into our circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow by what is prescribed by JNA protocol and procedure for the archiving and preservation of such log-books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, we did. However, given the fact that we did not have logistical support because it had not been dealt with in the best possible way by our competent command, we did the following: The typed-out encrypted report containing the conversation was the most important document leaving the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that certain log-books were destroyed or burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent correct. There was a whole sea of such notebooks from previous periods, from subordinate units, from the division, from our unit. It all burnt down. Well, it was used also to fuel fire, to roll cigarettes, et cetera. There were not only notebooks. It was mentioned in all of the trials here that the notebooks became widely available, especially in 1995. So we used different kinds of formats. From the northern facility, you'll see that they frequently have mining logs because it was -- it used to be a mining location, and they could only use one side of each sheet. In any case, we used anything that we could get our hands on just to note down information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe that you have stated that one operator would normally listen to the transmissions recorded on the tape through the UHER device for purposes of writing them down in a notebook but that others would be called in to listen to the tape with him if there was unclarity or question about a particular part that was hard to decipher. First of all, is there any notation or marking that would be visible on the notebook or on the typed report which would be generated from the notebooks which would denote these parts which were unclear and which had to be deciphered with the help of multiple persons listening to tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: If the question could be broken down. It's a very long question, and I just want to know -- first of all, I think it's fair to the witness if there were any notations or markings that would be visible in the notebook or the typed report, and if that could be -- if then a second question could be asked about the rest -- the remainder of the question. It's just a very run-on question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question, although being rather long, could be put in a short form to the witness and then to further elaborate on details. If one person had doubts as whether he could decipher what he heard and was then assisted by others to decipher, would that be noted down in the transcript or the document they created? Would it say I sought the assistance of A and B are or would it just result of it being jotted down on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was mainly as you conclude. Due to the rate of speech, two people may put headsets on their heads and listen together, and then they would try to reach a conclusion as to what the word used was and how the conversation developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then they jot it down, and that's how it would leave the facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it would not be noted that another person had also listened to that text. There was no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the recordings themselves, you have testified that there was a process by which re-recording of important communications on a different tape took place and then the old tapes were erased or dubbed over. I want to ask you first: Did this re-recording take place -- strike that. When this re-recording took place, who was it that decided what material was considered important enough to be saved on another tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained that several times. Whenever there was a change of shift, we took full tapes to the intelligence department when -- where they would be listened to again to verify or check the reports we had submitted by that time. They rerecorded the tapes that they believed were important in terms of the conversations they contained. We had nothing to do with it. It was also done for the sole purpose because we did not have enough tapes. If something was interested, it was rerecorded, and the rest would then be reused. So the tapes were returned to us. It was done for -- by the electronic warfare department which was within our intelligence unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to ask you at page 22 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before we start with new questions, if it would be one question, okay, but otherwise I would prefer to take the break first. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 10.30. We briefly go into closed session, then we'll resume after 20 minutes' break again in closed session so as to then return in open session once the witness has again entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 22 of the 92 ter transcript that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with you, sir, the testimony that's recorded at lines 7 through 11 of the same, and it reads as follows, and we should not broadcast the same, it is quoted as saying: "The reports were analysed in detail in the Analysis Department, and based on their analysis, guidelines were given for work. But, of course, every operator had to have an idea of how radio-relay systems in the VRS worked. So the process can at once appear simple and complicated." I want to ask you, when you say that the Analysis Department which was a part of military intelligence issued guidelines for the work, what kind of guidelines are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that there is no mistake, this analysis section is the counter-electronic warfare section. The guidelines were given for the most part for intensified reconnaissance if in a certain part of the front line increased activity was expected. If they had such information from other sources, they would give us instructions to pay more attention to the north, the south, south-east, because our zone was from north-west to south-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to the bottom of the page, and it bleeds onto the next page. Your answer reads as follows: "So primary analysis was made by our unit. Because of the frequency of traffic, we didn't have time for anything else. In the command of the 2nd Corps, there existed an Analysis Department, and opposite that department there existed a department for counter-intelligence protection which had the task of analysing all the information gathered through electronic reconnaissance and to fill out all the gaps in the communications system as it existed on the other side." Could you please tell us exactly what it means here to fill out all the gaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Considering that we were not the only unit engaged in electronic reconnaissance, this section, which is now here called anti-electronic activity, that's in fact counter-electronic warfare, received reports of this kind from intelligence sections of divisions, and they would put together the entire jigsaw puzzle for radio and relay communications in the area of the corps. That's why they put it this way. Fill in the gaps if, of course, we had information to fill in these gaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if we could now turn to the very last page of this document in e-court and still not broadcast the same. I'd like to focus on lines 11 through 14 of that page. And it read as follows: "We were not under any obligation to store these tapes and ... material recorded on them. The moment the intelligence section returned them, that meant they -- that they lost their importance. However, there was no time to erase everything. Some things were dubbed, some things remained on the tapes that were in use, and that happened in 1996 and 1997." Now, in relation to this testimony, would it sometimes result that conversations and recordings of old communications would blend into newer and subsequent recordings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened very rarely. If in the electronic warfare section they failed to erase it completely, we would do the erasing in our locations. During the transformation of the army in 1997, all the division units came to us with their own equipment. It simply didn't happen. There could be noise or interference only from the wear and tear of the tapes on which we made recordings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, in your answer here you have identified this in relation to the years 1996 and 1997. Am I correct that the same procedure was also employed in the years prior, including 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, because as I said before, I know exactly how things are properly done, but our logistics and our technical capabilities simply did not allow us to do it perfectly. We did our job as best we could. That was the only way to preserve things. I'll say again the reports bearing numbers are the official part of our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to look at another case with you, Popovic. If we can call up 1D1076, and page 5 of the same in e-court, and not broadcast the same just to be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: As the document is getting pulled up, I just wanted to make one minor transcript correction. It's on page 24, at line 19, and it's -- it goes: "The guidelines were given for the most part for intensified reconnaissance in certain part of the front line," and here it says "in a person part." And this is just to clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be obvious that there was a small mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can focus on line 13 and onwards to the bottom of the page, and I'd like to first read for you, sir, and then ask you some questions. "Q. We can now turn to a different topic. In response to the questions put to you by John Ostojic yesterday about what you said in your examination-in-chief, you said that in relation to certain persons, there existed already dossiers in which you wrote some of their features, their voices, and some of their personal features. Do you remember that? "A. Yes. "Q. And I suppose that this was done on the basis of long-term work and a large number of intercepts, that that was used to compile a dossier; right? "A. Yes. That's correct. I came to this unit in February of 1995 and there already existed a certain database for certain persons." I'd like to ask you, sir, do you stand by what is recorded here as being your testimony from the Popovic case as being both truthful and accurate such that you would so answer the same questions if posed today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes. I don't know what details you mean, but it's certain that we had a database for certain persons, mainly with information collected through electronic reconnaissance. This database covered mainly persons in the VRS involved in communications and the command staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could turn to the next page of this document. The continuation of the discussion there talks about at line 12: "Q. There are situations in which certain assumptions of operators were recorded, as you said, but that does not necessarily imply that they were correct. "A. Assumptions were confirmed at a higher level. They did not necessarily need to be correct, but were taken at face value, so that this -- so that was one of the positions taken." Do you stand by this portion of your testimony as recorded as being truthful and accurate such that you'd so testify today if asked the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say the same to these questions today. I'll repeat. Our job was to collect information as it was and submit it to the superior command, including our conclusions, suggestions, et cetera, which doesn't mean that the necessarily -- the superior command will take it at face value. It will accept it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I have for you, sir, is these reports and these notebooks that would be your end of it going up to the superior command, where would we look to find corrections, verifications, or nullifications by the higher authority about the assumptions that were made at the lower level, at the unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should look at the intelligence department. The commander never received information in the form of an intercept. It would first go to the counter-electronic warfare section, which would make their input, then to the analysis department of the intelligence department where they included their conclusions, and in a simplified form presented the information to the commander describing the situation on the ground. There were no major corrections or anything. It was simply a synthesis and an analysis of all the intelligence coming into one place from various sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and that's how I understood it. The question I have for you then is so these reports that are typed and these notebooks that we have from the unit are merely the assumptions by the unit, and we don't have any way of knowing what the verifications of the higher authority were, whether they found parts to be wrong, whether they found parts to be right. We can't find that out from these reports themselves. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would put it differently. These are not all assumptions. Assumptions are only certain parts of the report. And I'm going to say this again: This was a lengthy process over many years. In my mind these are facts that can be correct or incorrect. It's up to the higher level to decide what the essence is and what is not, because in addition to our information, they received information from other sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that the assumptions may not cover the entirety of the typed reports, but could you please enlighten us. How are we to identify those parts that are assumptions? Are they noticed in the documents in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how they marked it at the higher level, but I know from all that we did, 90 per cent was the truth, and I leave a 10 per cent margin for assumptions and certain errors [Realtime transcript read in error "in certain areas"], et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the higher authority. I'm asking about the unit. How did the unit mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the issue you're raising, the point you're making is perfectly clear to the Chamber at this point in time. I think the witness in various ways answered the question that he doesn't know how any acceptance or nonacceptance by the higher level would be visible in any of the reports. That's how I understood it. Therefore, you're pointing at certain risks that assumptions which were part of the reports may not have been visible and that therefore the Chamber should pay specific attention to the risks involved in that. If that's your point, then it's clear. If not, then please put focused questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I raise a problem for -- in the transcript. Page 30, line 4. I read there, I quote: "... I leave a 10 per cent margin for assumptions in certain areas, et cetera." I heard the -- a different answer from the witness. I thought you were talking about a 10 per cent margin for assumptions in certain -- and certain errors. Is that correct or what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Certain errors. Certain errors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, some errors in the work, omissions of a letter, misspelling, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to some technical aspects. First of all, would you agree with me that the VRS basically used pre-existing JNA radio relay systems, radio relay locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska did not use them more or less. They used all the assets and resources of the JNA. Only the roles were changed on paper. All that had already been installed and in place in the previous communications system me which had worked perfectly well for the 30 years before and longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would mean that you, your unit, knew where these pre-existing relay stations and transmission stations were located. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, let's not talk about assumptions. I told you we had one man in our installation in the south, and we knew about all the -- these things. We did not know which radio relay asset was exactly in which

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not Zepa but Zep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the radio relay communications from Vlasenica to Veliki Zep to Zvornik were conducted using radio relay devices RRU 800 and SMC 1306B over four radio relay routes or RR sub-D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with what you stated here, but I'm saying again it was our opinion that we reached by just monitoring radio relay communications and occasionally we would check the strength of the signal across the entire range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that communications from -- by the VRS from Vlasenica to Veliki Zep were performed via a RRU 800 and that the distance between the two was approximately 15 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I would just like it to be clarified to the witness. I mean, we're talking about equipments taken from the JNA, and so I would like to know the time-frame. Are we talking about in -- I mean, what year are we talking about? Are we talking about in 1995 or are we talking about sometime before that? And if that could be put to the witness just for clarification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you willing to adopt the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, these radio locations of the former JNA that you said even little children knew, did they change at all during the time-period when the unit was in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've told you the main hubs did not change. The only thing that changed were end radio relay stations of individual brigades. These are specialised installations that cost a lot of money, including atomic shelters, huge stocks, et cetera. That's not something you create in one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I ask you again, sir, from the installation at Vlasenica to the installation at Veliki Zep that the distance between the two was 15 kilometres and that the device that was installed there was a RRU 800.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to our information, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused now. I think I earlier asked what an RRU would be. Would that be a specific device, or would that be a device which would cover a certain frequency. Now, Mr. Ivetic, did you intend to ask whether the device installed was fit to cover the RRU 800 range of frequency? Is that -- or did you have a specific installation, a specific equipment in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the installation at both the Vlasenica pre-existing station of the JNA and the Veliki Zep pre-existing installation of the JNA which both operated a RRU 800 and that the physical distance between those two locations was 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a few questions in one. Let's first start with the -- with the distance. Is it 15 kilometres between Vlasenica and Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say exactly, but if we had a map, we would calculate it easily. It's around 15. As the crow flies, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second, the equipment at Veliki Zep, was that of the RRU 800 type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the pieces of equipment at Veliki Zep was RRU 800. It's the size of a small cupboard, rather heavy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, in relation to the installation at Veliki Zep and the installation at Cer, am I correct that the distance as the crow flies is approximately 70.7 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with you, yes. It's around -- around that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that according to your information, the communications done on that route would have been by the SMC 1306B because of the distance involved, and so that is it exceeds the RRU 800's capabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with you. This SMC 1306B was used because that was one of the main communications with Belgrade. SMC 130 is high quality, it has a more directed antenna, and it's safer for maintaining communication, plus it has 116 channels that can operate simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct that the other device at Veliki Zep was also a RRU 1 radio relay device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what we know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you know, would you agree that from the Cer installation to Crni Vrh, the air distance as the crow flies is approximately 28 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't measure, but it's around that distance, Vlasenica, and up there is Sabac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and was there, as you understood it, two RRU 800 devices on Crni Vrh elevation with communications going towards the Zvornik -- going towards Zvornik and from Zvornik by that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how many devices there were at Crni Vrh, but we know from monitoring long-term communications that at Crni Vrh, at Mount Gucevo, there was one RRU 800, and since Zvornik is in a valley near the Drina River, it had a direct communication with this end radio relay station. And what's more, from our information, I remember this clearly, from Zvornik and up there they provided crews to their personnel. It must be written somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that all the radio relay communications devices that we are talking about are for duplex communications, meaning a communication as a distinct transmission and reception direction or telephone channel on the entire external communication route, meaning that communications on one radio relay route is conducted using two different radio frequencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you. There is a receiving and transmitting frequency with the RRU 800, as well as with the RRU 1, which is a radio relay device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Great. Now I'd like to clear up some more matters. In your Rule 92 ter transcript P1614 under seal, page 15, and it's lines 8 through 25 that are recorded there that are for me, I think, also a translation, perhaps, issue, because it's not clear which devices you're identifying and which comments about your abilities as to the devices are accurate. So to clear it up, I'd like to talk about the technical aspects and see if we can reach some agreement. First of all, on the route of Vlasenica-Veliki Zep, there was a radio relay device, an RRU 800, which transmitted 24 telephone channels, namely two primary groups from which one group ended in Veliki Zep and the second group was forwarded to Cer by way of the SMC 1306B relay and further to Sazbrenica [phoen] over a JNA -- over the JNA system. Is that -- does that comport with your knowledge of the communications that were underway on that system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would agree with you again. It was normal to change a lower frequency to a higher frequency. That's why the devices were used, and it is rather difficult to explain in technical terms, speaking from memory. In any case, from Vlasenica there was an RRU 800, and then further to Cer we used an SMC. That was because we were never able to either locate or monitor that frequency range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to correct something. I think you had testified accurately but that the transcript may have an error. It is said that -- that further to Cer, we used an SMC. Was it "we" the ABiH that used the SMC or was it the VRS that used the SMC, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The VRS, not the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, the SMC 1306B that we're talking about is a dual device that transmits and receives working with frequencies of 4.4 to 4.6 gigahertz and 4.8 to 5.0 gigahertz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the ABiH did not have the technology required to intercept communications which used this device set-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the ABiH, but my unit did not have that possibility. We had an old device which I believe we had received from Travnik. It was an SMC, but we were never successful in making it operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is the SMC 1306B a system that employs so-called satellite frequencies and is used when there is no optical and therefore no radio visibility between two points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that characteristic. I know it's a radio relay device and that one needs a clear line of vision. In other words, there should be no obstacles between the two end points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there optical and therefore radio visibility between Veliki Zep and Zvornik between the radio end points at those two installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have in mind Veliki Zep and the end point radio relay station in Zvornik, there was no optical vision. That's why the alternative was used via Cer and Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the RRU 1 device or system was not utilised during the period of June to August 1995 on the territory of Vlasenica to Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or deny that. The RRU 1 radio relay device is something at that can be put on one's back and carried to whatever place you want, as long as you can mount an antenna and to be within the range of Veliki Zep or another radio relay hub. It can also establish direct communication between two radio relay devices of the same kind if there is optical visibility. It's a single-channel device, so it receives and transmits on one channel only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in radio parlance that would be called a simplex veza [phoen], or simplex device; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we're also clear, this RRU 1 device that we're both talking about manufactured in Iskra factory in Ljubljana operated on -- in simplex mode on a frequency of 300 to 340 hertz, and then if it was used in a duplex mode it would have been on the principle of frequent modulation in the range of 235 to 270 megahertz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was produced in Slovenia, so it was of domestic production. Its working frequency is the second one you mentioned between 235 and 270 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in -- in relation to this RRU 1 device working on that frequency, am I correct that the range of coverage of the same, of the signal from the same, is about 30 kilometres from the centre and the receiver unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the textbooks I believe that is what is stated, but I have to repeat yet again: Each manufacturer provides the characteristics of a device where they guarantee that it will function within that range and at that distance. It doesn't mean, though, that communication cannot be established at bigger distances. Electromagnetic waves are not something tangible. You never know how far they can go. It depends on a number of factors. For example, for the RRU 800 they say that the range is up to 80, but it can reach as far as 120 or 130 kilometres depending on the lie of land and whether there are depressions or features on the way -- in the way. Perhaps I don't need to repeat everything now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And weather conditions would also affect it, temperature, et cetera? Pardon me, sun activity, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there's a number of factors, time of day, whether it is day or night, vegetation, humidity, whether it is overcast. It all has an impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now in this part of your Rule 92 ter transcript, you also mention the HVT 1 device that operated between 400 and 500 megahertz but it's a little unclear as to this device whether in fact your unit had the ability to intercept this device or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already answered saying that our unit could not follow the SMC, HVT 1, and FM 200, so frequency modulation, which is also used for radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take the last two one by one. With respect to the HVT 1, was this also a device manufactured in the Ljubljana Iskra factory with a maximum range of 50 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't read about its specifications, but as far as I recall, it is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you are talking about factory specifications. You earlier explained to us that the range in kilometres given by the factory would be a guaranteed range but that it may well go beyond that depending on all the circumstances you mentioned, including atmospheric circumstances. Where you answered the question about the maximum range, did you -- where you said you did not know, would you consider such a factory specification in similar terms as you explained to us before as to whether it really was limited to a given range or whether it could go beyond or perhaps under circumstances stay below that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. President. These are the technical specifications of a device. When a factory produces a device, they say you can establish communication up to 80 kilometres. If you place two stations within that range, they guarantee that the device will work properly, which in our parlance means, although it is not guaranteed by the factory, that their device can reach up to 100 or 120 kilometres if there are no significant features in the way such as mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maximum range means maximum guaranteed range by the factory. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for these guaranteed ranges, according to the specifications of the factory, that would be for a brand new device capable of powering up to 100 per cent. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, this question is something to ponder, but a new device with good characteristics and all the necessary checks should, with maximum power, establish communication without any problems at the specified range, which doesn't mean that it could not reach such communication with less capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could focus on the RRU 800 for a moment. That device was new in the 1950s and 1960s, and in 1995 was already considered an old-fashioned device. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for Europe it was old fashioned. If you take into account that it worked, say, four [as interpreted] hours a day for over 40 years, one could definitely not say that it is at its best any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask there one question. The device was new in the 1950s and 1960s. Does that mean that they were not produced at any later point in time, or were they still produced but were they old fashioned as far as the technology was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our view and to my knowledge, that device was produced at the time specified, and later they may have been still produced but to a less -- lesser degree, because the system had to be changed at all mountain tops of Yugoslavia if you wanted a completely new system. That is why this system lived such a long time. It's a costly enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one clarification. It's entered into the transcript, sir, that these devices would be working four hours a day. Did you say four hours or 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you agree that the RRU 800 in 1995 that worked out of a double exploitation period and had a maximum outgoing strength that was about 70 per cent of the original value?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: If this is a statement of fact, if that could be put to the witness. I'm not -- I'm wondering how this witness could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since he testified to it in other trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Then can that portion be put to him or read to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not see why the witness couldn't answer the question. The witness is asked whether he agrees that the RRU 800 in 1995, that -- and that's the assumption, not yet been established, although almost confirmed by the witness, that worked out of a double exploitation period, there Mr. Ivetic apparently referred to the 40 or 50 years, and he apparently has in his mind that the exploitation period was approximately half of that, that as a result the maximum outgoing strength was about 70 per cent of the original value. Ms. Lee, I do agree with you that Mr. Ivetic includes in his question a series of assumptions, but at the same time, having listened to the evidence of this witness, there is at least some basis for such assumptions. Now, I have rephrased the question for you, Witness. Could you tell us on the basis of all the assumptions included in this question whether you would agree that the strength of the original value had been reduced to 70 per cent -- about 70 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There may be -- may be an interpretation problem here. As I read the question as formulated by Mr. Ivetic, it doesn't seem complete because of the conjunction "and," and this thing is supposed to have -- be an RRU 800 in 1995 and worked out of double exploitation and had maximum outgoing strength of 70 per cent value, so what is the question after that? These are all -- these are all assumptions. The question has not been put yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are all assumptions. Mr. Ivetic, the way in which I rephrased the question, did that reflect what you had on your mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but what you did not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it more eloquently stated the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, more precisely I would say. Eloquence is not my strongest. Witness, have you followed the way in which I rephrased the question, and would you agree then that after 40 to 50 years that it would be 70 per cent which remains as, if I could say so, the power or the strength? I think strength was the word used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I recall the question being put in the Popovic case when Defence claimed that the devices were so old that they were only at half strength, and I said that in our view if the devices were used for 40 years that their strength was down to between 70 -- was down by 70 to 80 per cent, meaning that only 30 to 40 per cent were left, which is impossible. That was the question put in that case. I still believe that two persons, one aged 20 and another aged 60, could not produce the same results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a mysterious answer for me. Do you mean that if something is older that does not necessarily mean that the capacity, even if it's worn out quite a bit, that the capacity does not have necessarily to have been substantially reduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in any case or every case, but in most cases we have to agree. I'm not the same person I was 30 years ago. Defence claimed that all of the devices we monitored worked in the middle of the war with a reduced strength, which is absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you is it the kind of discussion if whether you drive an old car whether it loses maximum velocity, maximum speed. It may do a bit, a car which was produced for driving 150 kilometres might end up after 20 years in driving 140 kilometres or 130, but not necessarily much further down. Is that the kind of thought that is behind your mysterious answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Wear and tear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to ask the mysterious answer be clarified. Sir, you said at temporary transcript page 43, lines 11 through 12: "And I said that in our view if the devices were used for 40 years, that their strength was down to between 70 -- was down by 70 to 80 per cent." Could you please explain that answer in terms of -- first of all, when you say "in our view," are you referring to the unit of the ABiH that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The officers and the people we discussed here, they were probably people who were more familiar with the devices themselves. If something has been working for 40 years nonstop, of course it's a degree of exploitation, its strength is different, and no one can claim otherwise. From the Popovic context, when we discussed about it, I remember they said that all of the devices worked at only half strength which is absurd. This is what I meant. If --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat the end of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said this is what I meant, and then you started another sentence. Could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that from the context concerning the people we talked about -- talked with when discussing the manuals, it was concluded that a device working for 40 years has a difference in power and strength and that its strength is no longer the same. The other side claimed that all of those devices in 1995 worked at half strength. So if it used its exploitation strength in the height of the war when you depend on your communications, if they indeed worked at only half strength, then it would have struck me as illogical from a military standpoint. It would mean that they worked at one-third of their strength, and which would mean that we couldn't even monitor such devices because they could only transmit at very low strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that what you're saying is that if the strength was so drastically reduced, it could not serve its purpose as communication channels any further because it couldn't bridge the distances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only repeating the claims made by the Defence when we discussed this issue. They claimed that these already old devices, 40-year-old devices, were working at only half strength, meaning with a loss of 50 per cent of their original capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Making them unfit to perform what they were supposed to perform. Is that what I understand would be the result of such a claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Precisely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. Before we take a -- yes. Judge Moloto has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. Now, because I didn't -- your answers were not very clear to me, and apparently they were described as mysterious, I just want to ask you: You say the opposite side in the Popovic case claimed that [indiscernible] equipment worked at 50 per cent strength. In your view, at what strength did they work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our opinion, it was working with a 70, 80 of -- per cent of its original capacity, as new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first move into closed session, and resume after the break in closed session so as to allow the witness to leave and enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, so that we can explain to persons who may not have experience with military-grade or professional-grade radio equipment, am I correct that for such equipment there is more than merely a power on-off switch, but there is also a power modulation knob that allows you to adjust the power setting for that particular radio transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean professional military equipment, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in respect specifically to the RRU 800 professional military equipment, that device has or had a power variable knob allowing the operator to decrease the power output to that machine to something less than 100 per cent of its capacity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that in the JNA radio operators were trained and, in fact, it was part of an obligatory counter-electronic protection method of the JNA that when operating a RRU 800 over ranges shorter than its guaranteed maximum, the power settings would be reduced so as to limit the opportunity for opposing forces to intercept those communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me that in terms of covering the shorter relay radio sections such as Vlasenica installation to Veliki Zep of approximately 15 kilometres, Zvornik installation to Crni Vrh installation approximately 10.5 kilometres, and Cer location to Crni Vrh installation of 28.2 kilometres, RRU 800 devices would only need to operate at approximately 50 per cent of their maximum power to accomplish covering those short distances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with you in one part but not in another. I don't know with what strength they were working. All I know is that we were listening to them. Whether they used 50, 70, or 100 per cent of their capacity, I don't know, but we listened to them, and all that we heard is written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me about the technical capabilities and the method trained by the JNA for the use of the device that to cover those shorter ranges the operator would reduce the power output and that would be sufficient to cover those shorter ranges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness has answered this question by, in principle, yes, and then he explains that he didn't know what was done and that, of course, that keeps you apart. The witness thinking in terms of what he knows rather than in theory, and he explained that what was the case he doesn't know, he only knows that that was listened. But I think he already agreed that this was part of the training, that this was the principle, the theory. So therefore -- and I see the witness is nodding yes, so apparently he agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He confirms it by saying, "Yes, yes." So the witness has answered at that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- we sort of went off track to talk to the specifics of the RRU 800. We left off also talking about one more advice -- device which you had identified which was the FM 200, which your unit could not intercept, and just to make sure we're talking about the same device and understand each other, is the FM 200 the device that was obtained by the JNA in 1975 to begin replacing the RRU 800 produced by the west German firm of Siemens and Telefunken? Let's start with that as the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer. I can only suppose. You should ask someone from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. I know that a replacement should have been done. Whether it was at that stage FM 200 or some other device, it's a frequency modulated signal, whereas the RRU was analogue. That's why we were able to listen to it. RRU had a modulated signal, and we didn't have the equipment to monitor it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction: FM had a modulated signal and that's why we didn't have the equipment to monitor it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the FM 200 also required optical and radio visibility and had a factory -- factory guaranteed range of 50 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really wouldn't like to go into detailed technical specifications. You can find that on the internet. But all radio relay devices require optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could briefly go into private session I have some questions that relate specifically to the locations of the stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As a general guidance to the parties, if we're talking about distances, take a map and a cup of tea and a cup of coffee and establish what the distances are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I wish to focus on the equipment or actually -- pardon me, the antenna that were at the various listening posts that were used by the ABiH both the northern and the southern positions, and I'd like to do the southern position first. Am I correct that this location had four monitoring posts that used the following devices: First, two ICR 100 attached to a logoperiodic antenna; one ICR 100 attached to a parabolic antenna; and one AR 3000A attached to a parabolic antenna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately. That was approximately what was needed to cover the equipment we had. I cannot remember every specific unit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we could be perhaps fair to the witness, I'd like to not broadcast but call up in e-court 1D1081.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, as I ask you these questions, I can -- I can refer you to this document that is dated the 15th of February, 1995, and I believe that you are familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we -- I think we only have this one in B/C/S so perhaps -- oh, we do have the translation. I apologise. But we may need to go to the last page to allow the witness to identify why he might recognise this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, actually, do you recognise this document, sir? The sender and the recipients are the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we go back to the first page. Here it is recorded, sir, that the unit in question had -- that both parabolic antenna had an SO 42 converter attached to them, and I want to ask you in respect to the SO 42 converter, is it correct that such a converter is not generally needed nor used for frequencies ranges below 1 gigahertz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. These converters that we had were mainly handmade, and they were used -- it's a bit technically difficult to explain. Our equipment was not professional. First of all, we had to raise frequency to 16.000 megahertz, I believe, to use as a 0 baseline. So it's not the same baseline for our devices and military devices. We had to raise the signal. These are all makeshift converters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this document says that the SO 42 converters were attached, it is not, in fact, what is in the industry generally acknowledged as an SO 42 converter. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you put the question to the witness. Could you explain to this Chamber exactly what it is that you asked? So the witness apparently understood it, but for the Chamber, you are referring to a certain -- you said the SO 42 converters were attached but they were not, in fact, what in the industry generally acknowledge as an SO 42 converter. Could you tell us what is in the industry is generally acknowledged as an SO 42 converter and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, an SO 42 converter is an addition or an add-on to an existing antenna array that allows you to convert signals that are in excess of 1 gigahertz so that you can listen to them on devices that do not go in that range. Now, the Defence position, Your Honours, is that since all the devices that we've talked about that were used by the JNA, that were used by the VRS, are all under 1 gigahertz, that the addition of this converter was not anything that would assist these antenna to intercept these devices and these signals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore we should ask the witness first of all whether he agrees with you that what is generally acknowledged as an SO 42 converter is that that applies only or exclusively to add-ons which allow to convert signals that are in excess of 1 gigahertz. So you can listen them on devices that do not go to that range. Is that your understanding of what an SO 42 converter is as explained by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's a bit complicated to explain these technical things. This converter was not exactly outside by the antenna. These converters were behind the device and the preamplifiers. The preamplifiers were used to increase the signal, and the converters were used to adapt to the frequency. They were not -- because our devices were not calibrated the same as military equipment. I don't know how else to explain it, although I know the function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate your explanation, but my question was the way -- because this Chamber, of course, is not familiar with SO 42 converters as they are produced in the normal industry, whether you agreed with Mr. Ivetic that you were talking about the same as he was talking about, and that's the reason why I asked him to explain what he understood to be an industrial, not your ones but the industrial SO 42 converters, being add-ons which are used if the frequency is above 1 megahertz I think it was -- gigahertz, and to reduce that. Is that usually the -- what you understand industrially as an SO 42 converter? Again, not your ones, but as produced normally. Is that an accurate description of what an SO 42 converter is, the description given by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he found this information from legitimate sources, some authorities, so to that extent I would agree, but in this case the function the converter is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is the general understanding of what an SO 42 converter is, the way in which Mr. Ivetic explain that. Again, not yours, but in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Ivetic, for the Chamber to understand the technicalities, and we try hard, it's good to -- to use such terms that are understandable and not only code-names. What an industrial SO 42 converter is may be a shared secret between you and the witness, but if you want the Chamber to pay attention to it, just try to translate it in ordinary terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
